analysis.one_liner: Gives hourly retail, food service, and similar workers two weeks' notice of schedules and pay when employers change them late.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025, with 21 Democratic and Independent cosponsors, and was referred to the Senate labor committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets just-in-time scheduling, where employers post work schedules with little notice, cancel shifts at the last minute, and assign on-call or back-to-back closing-then-opening shifts. It would require employers with 15 or more workers to give retail, food service, cleaning, hotel, and warehouse employees their schedules at least 14 days ahead, pay extra ($75 per day, plus premium pay) when schedules change on short notice, pay for split shifts, and give workers the right to request schedule changes for caregiving, health, school, or a second job without retaliation. It also bars requiring employees to work fewer than 11 hours after a shift ends without written consent and premium pay, and lets the Labor Department enforce with civil penalties and lets workers sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers in retail, food service, cleaning, hospitality, and warehouses — about two-thirds of whom get less than two weeks' schedule notice today — plus their families, who gain stable child care, transportation, and second-job planning.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly retail, food service, and warehouse workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give covered workers their schedules at least 14 days in advance and pay $75 per employee per day for every day a schedule is late.
Employers who change a schedule with less than 14 days' notice must pay an extra hour of pay for added or moved shifts, and half-time pay for hours the employer cancels.

Workers may request schedule changes for a serious health condition, caregiving, schooling, or a second job, and employers must grant them unless they have a bona fide business reason to deny; retaliation for requesting is unlawful.
Workers may decline shifts starting less than 11 hours after their previous shift ends, or must be paid 1.5 times their rate if they consent to work them.

Workers get one extra hour of pay for any day with a split shift, and enforcement includes Labor Department penalties ($500–$5,000 per violation) and private lawsuits with liquidated damages and attorney's fees.

analysis.who_pays: Large retail chains, restaurant and fast-food operators, hotels, janitorial companies, and warehouse operators, which would face schedule-posting duties, premium pay for late changes and split shifts, and potential penalties — costs they currently avoid through just-in-time scheduling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retail, restaurant, hotel, and warehouse employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on scheduling-intensive businesses: the $75-per-day late-schedule charge, an extra hour of pay per last-minute change, split-shift pay, and 1.5x pay for clopening shifts would raise labor costs or force more rigid staffing, and some of that cost may show up in prices or reduced flexibility for small franchise operators.

The 14-day posting rule gives workers fewer tools than they might want: an employer may still change a posted schedule at any time if it pays the premium, and the bill exempts workers covered by a union contract that expressly waives its terms.

The right-to-request process requires the employer to deny only with a 'bona fide business reason', but the worker bears the burden of challenging that denial in practice, so the right depends on enforcement resources and litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest: the bill converts unpredictable, unpaid schedule instability — which the bill's findings tie to worse sleep, mental health, child-care chaos, hunger, and housing insecurity, and which falls hardest on low-paid workers and workers of color — into a modest, predictable cost for large employers, which its own findings cite evidence (including a Gap Inc. experiment) suggesting can be offset by lower turnover and higher sales. The premium-pay rates are calibrated to discourage last-minute changes without banning them, and small employers under 15 workers are exempt. The main honest objection is cost pass-through in thin-margin industries; the main design limit is that the right-to-request provision is only as strong as workers' willingness to enforce it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced near the end of the first session and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which has not acted on it; it has not had a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on December 17, 2025, joined by 20 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history as of this writing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has happened, so the status quo benefits employers who rely on just-in-time scheduling; the bill's fate rests with the Senate labor committee, whose leadership has not taken it up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using just-in-time scheduling, for now

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Schedules That Work Act on December 17, 2025.

for.name: 20 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (19 Democrats, 1 Independent), including Senators Blumenthal, Sanders, Schumer, Klobuchar, Durbin, and Fetterman
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a Democratic and Independent Senate bloc of 21.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 supporters are Democrats or Independents; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill sits with the Senate committee of jurisdiction without a hearing or vote.

industries.note: Covered retail sales occupations must get 14-day schedules, $75-per-day late charges, predictability pay for late changes, and split-shift pay — replacing just-in-time staffing that keeps labor costs down by shifting uncertainty onto workers.
Food preparation and serving occupations are squarely covered; last-minute shift changes, on-call shifts, and split shifts are common in the industry and would now carry premium pay.
Hospitality establishments are explicitly covered, including cleaning staff, with the same notice and premium-pay requirements.
Warehouse establishments are covered; the bill was written partly with erratic warehouse scheduling in mind, so operators would face posting rules and premium pay for schedule churn.
Janitors, cleaners, and housekeeping staff are covered occupations subject to the notice, predictability-pay, and rest-between-shifts rules.

analysis.trajectory: With 21 Democratic and Independent cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill is unlikely to advance through the Senate labor committee or reach a floor vote in the remainder of this Congress. Similar fair-scheduling proposals have repeatedly stalled at this stage; the most likely path is that it stays in committee unless labor scheduling becomes a priority in a future spending or workforce bill.
